title: Lightning talk | Mapping the plandemic
description:
The COVID-19 conspiracy video “Plandemic” was one of the defining viral disinformation events of 2020. The slickly produced, self-styled “documentary” featured a former research scientist active in anti-vaccine activist circles as an authority figure and was announced ahead of time by its producers to build anticipation. Within hours of its premiere, “Plandemic” racked up hundreds of millions of views online. By the time major platforms took action to limit its spread, the video had gained hold across the entrenched ecosystem of niche conspiracy communities and spread across smaller hosting in anticipation of its removal from Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter. In this talk, DFRLab researchers will discuss how the trajectory of “Plandemic” serves as an important case study for how disinformation spreads, the challenges and limits of content moderation focused on specific pieces of viral content, and how different communities respond to platform enforcement.

Speaker:
Zarine Kharazian, Associate Editor, Digital Forensic Research Lab, Atlantic Council

title: ‘Plandemic’ Planet: Battling the Infodemic #CyFy2020
description:
From heads of state to terrorists, there is no shortage of actors willing to manipulate platforms to create and amplify mis- and disinformation. The Covid-19 pandemic has fed into an existing infodemic, further damaging the digital public sphere. This is a global problem, with research suggesting that malicious actors are increasingly “bandwagoning” onto each other’s information operations. Although states have begun to address to the crisis of mis- and disinformation, global responses remain disparate and fragmented. How can states, platforms and communities balance tensions between national legal regimes and international rights frameworks in cyberspace?

title: PLANDEMIC - Who should we trust?
description:
#BudgetCreator  #Plandemic  #SmallYoutuber
So recently a video entitled Plandemic surfaced on social media platforms. In this video, American ex-research scientist Judy Anne Mikovits made a series of stunning claims which she said will expose the scientific and political elite who run the scam that is our global health system.
The 26 minute video immediately went viral and after just a couple days it had already amassed 1.8 million views and 150,000 shares on Facebook as well as over 4.7 million views on Youtube. Facebook and Youtube have labeled content like this as dangerous misinformation and scrambled to delete these videos but they just kept on popping up.
This led me to ask these questions… Why is it so difficult for platforms such as Facebook, Youtube and even Twitter to get rid of misinformation and Should these videos be kept on these platforms under the banner of “Free Speech?”

The difficulty in removing these videos

The first reason why it is so difficult to get rid of misinformation is due to the limitations of automated moderation tools. A perfect example is Facebook filters marking what was deemed to be legitimate Covid-19 news as spam which left many users upset. Due to the increasing need to observe social distancing protocols during this pandemic, companies are now reliant on Artificial Intelligence more than ever.
The second reason is that videos can be shared millions of times before being labelled. Even after being removed, users can simply edit and reupload these videos. By doing this, the algorithm will see this as a new video which will allow it to get even more shares before it is eventually removed again. By then, tens of millions or even hundreds of millions of people could have seen it.
The third reason is labelling videos as content of misinformation simply doesn’t work. In fact, it does the opposite. Humans are naturally curious creatures and so if you tell someone that this video contains sensitive information, you can bet your last silver coin that they will click on it.

Why did this video cause such a stir?

First let us take a look at some of the claims made by Judy Mikovits:
-Judy said wearing a mask could make you sick because it could expose you to your own reactivated coronavirus expressions.
-‘She claims This occurred from SARS 1 within a decade which means it’s not naturally occurring’

-It’s very clear this virus was manipulated.

title: American Conspiracy Theories - Joseph Uscinski, University of Miami
description:
This talk is part of the 2022 ICPSR Blalock Lecture Series.

Questions from this lecture:

- How is a conspiracy theory different from any other theory?

The word theory can mean lots of things. Conspiracy theory is an assertion of a conspiracy that has yet to be accepted as true by the appropriate epistemological authorities with open data and evidence.

I spend a chapter on the definition here: https://www.amazon.com/Conspiracy-Theories-Primer-Joseph-Uscinski/dp/1538121204

- I know that part of the issue regarding the measurement and comparison of conspiracy theory trends over time is the lack of prior survey data. What other ways could scholars measure conspiracy theory deeper into the past? Specifically, I’m interested in how to separate coverage and belief in times that don’t have survey data

In the past I have tried letters to the editor of newspapers: https://www.amazon.com/American-Conspiracy-Theories-Joseph-Uscinski/dp/0199351813/ref=pd_lpo_2?pd_rd_i=0199351813&psc=1

Other studies look at comments sections in online newspapers: https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00409/full

- Great talk, Joe! Are you able to share any insight on sub-group differences in the propensity to hold conspiratorial beliefs? For example, differences based on one's race, gender, educational attainment, etc.?

Yes: Chapter 4 here: https://www.amazon.com/American-Conspiracy-Theories-Joseph-Uscinski/dp/0199351813/ref=pd_lpo_2?pd_rd_i=0199351813&psc=1
